13850: A sluice is a structure built to control the flow of water. Think of it as a "water door" — one that can be opened to let water rush through, or closed to hold it back. Everything about this word comes back to that one idea: deliberately managing water so it flows in a controlled way.

Picture a wall, dam, or solid embankment built across a river, canal, or pond. In that wall, there is an opening. Fitted tightly into that opening is a sliding gate or panel — this is the heart of the sluice. The gate sits in a frame, and it can be raised, lowered, or slid to one side. When you open it, water pours through the gap. When you close it, the water is stopped. The whole assembly — the gate, its frame, and the passage through which water flows — is what we call a sluice.

Imagine you are holding your thumb halfway over a garden hose nozzle. By adjusting how much you cover it, you control the speed and direction of the water. A sluice does the same thing, but on a large, permanent scale for outdoor waterways. By raising or lowering the gate, people can control how fast the water moves, raise or lower the water level on one side, and redirect water into a particular channel.

Sluices appear almost anywhere humans need to manage water.

On canals, canal locks use sluice gates to raise and lower the water level in small sections so that boats can travel smoothly between stretches of water at different heights. On rivers and flood plains, sluices built into embankments can be closed during floods to protect low-lying land, and opened during dry spells to allow normal flow. At old water mills, the miller would open a sluice to direct river water onto a large wheel, which then powered the mill — opening the sluice started the mill working, and closing it brought the wheel to a stop. On farms, sluices in irrigation channels let farmers direct water to fields when needed and cut it off when not. At reservoirs and dams, sluices allow engineers to release water in safe, measured amounts rather than letting it build up and overflow dangerously.
The three things "sluice" can refer to

When people use the word, they may be pointing to one of three closely related things.

First, the gate itself — the physical sliding or hinged panel that opens and closes. This is often called a "sluice gate" but is frequently just called a "sluice." If someone says "they lifted the sluice," they mean they raised this gate.

Second, the channel or passage — the artificial opening or waterway through which the controlled water flows. If someone says "water rushed through the sluice," they mean the passageway the water travels through.

Third, the entire structure as one unit — the gate, its framework, and the channel all working together. In this sense, "the sluice" means the whole water-control system at that point in a waterway.

All three usages are correct and common. Context usually makes it clear which one is meant, and since they are all parts of the same thing, the distinction rarely causes confusion.
A special case: the mining sluice

In gold mining, the word takes on a slightly different shape. A mining sluice (also called a sluice box) is a long, narrow, inclined trough — usually made of wood or metal — through which water is continuously run. Miners shovel gravel and soil into this trough. The rushing water carries away the lighter sand and dirt, while heavier gold particles sink and get trapped by small ridges fixed to the bottom of the trough (called riffles). In this case there is no gate — the sluice is simply the channel that uses flowing water to do the separating work. The shared idea with the gate-type sluice is still there: water is being deliberately directed through a channel to accomplish a purpose.

Whether you are talking about a gate in a dam, a channel in a canal, or a trough on a hillside mine, the word "sluice" always carries these ideas together: water moving through a defined opening or passage, and that flow being deliberately designed and controlled by people. It is never accidental water — it is always managed water.

"The farmer walked over to the sluice and slowly pulled the gate upward, flooding the paddy field within minutes."

"A torrent of cold water burst through the sluice when the operator lost control of the gate."

"The old mill pond fed into a narrow sluice that carried water directly onto the turning wheel below."

"The gold miners built a rough wooden sluice along the hillside stream and spent the afternoon shovelling gravel into it, watching the current carry the dirt away."

"Engineers inspected every sluice along the riverbank before the rainy season began, making sure each gate could seal tightly enough to protect the town downstream."
13851: To sluice something means to wash or clean it using a large, forceful rush of water — the kind of washing where water doesn't just trickle or drip, but floods over a surface with power and speed, sweeping everything in its path away. Think of the difference between dabbing a muddy boot with a damp cloth versus holding it under a powerful outdoor tap and letting the gushing water blast the mud right off. That second action — the forceful, flooding wash — is sluicing.
The Two Ways the Verb is Used

1. When YOU do the sluicing to something (you are in control, directing the water)

This is the most common use. You point a large flow of water at something to clean it or rinse it thoroughly. The action is deliberate — you are the one releasing or directing the water.

  • A fisherman returns to the dock and sluices down the bloody deck with a bucket of seawater.
  • A farmer sluices out the animal stalls, flooding the floor with water to wash away the filth.
  • A tired hiker sluices her face with cold water from a stream.
  • A chef sluices the cutting board under a hard running tap after breaking down raw meat.

In every case, notice: lots of water, applied with force, with a cleansing purpose.

2. When water itself is the subject — it sluices on its own

Here, you use "sluice" to describe water (or any liquid) rushing, streaming, or pouring in a powerful, unrestrained flow — usually through a narrow point or across a surface. The water is behaving like it has just been released through a gate.

  • Rainwater sluiced down the steep rooftop and crashed into the gutters.
  • Muddy water sluiced through the canyon after the storm.
  • Tears sluiced down her cheeks. (a literary, expressive use — writers sometimes extend the word to any liquid flowing freely and fast)
What Makes "Sluice" Different from Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so let's sharpen the definition against words that feel similar.

Sluice vs. Wash — "Wash" is a broad, everyday word for cleaning with water. It has no particular force, speed, or volume implied. You can wash a cup gently. You cannot gently sluice anything — sluicing always involves abundance and power.

Sluice vs. Rinse — "Rinse" means to pass water over something to remove soap or loose dirt. It's light and brief. Sluicing is heavier, more forceful, and more thorough. You rinse a glass; you sluice a fish market floor.

Sluice vs. Flush — These are close. "Flush" often implies pushing something through a pipe or channel (flush a toilet, flush a wound). "Sluice" is more about flooding over or across a surface, though there is genuine overlap in some cases.

Sluice vs. Drench/Douse — These mean to soak something heavily with water, but they don't carry the sense of directional flow or cleaning. You drench someone accidentally. You sluice something deliberately as a cleaning act.

The unique flavour of "sluice" is this combination: a large volume of water + significant force + a sense of directed flow + usually a cleansing purpose.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

"Sluice" is a strong, physical, vivid word. It belongs to working environments — harbours, farms, mines, kitchens, construction sites — places where real mess exists and real force is needed to deal with it. When a writer chooses "sluice" over "wash," they are deliberately painting a picture of power, volume, and urgency. It is not a delicate word.

When used about liquid flowing on its own ("rain sluiced down the street"), the word creates a strong visual: water moving fast, in volume, unstoppably — the way a floodgate being opened might release a sudden rush.

One specific historical and still-used context is worth knowing. In gold mining, miners would sluice gravel — they would direct a powerful stream of water through a long angled trough (the trough itself also called a sluice) filled with gravel from a riverbed. The rushing water would carry away the lighter sand and gravel, while the heavier gold particles sank and were caught. This process is called sluicing, and it remains one of the most iconic uses of the word. It perfectly illustrates the verb: a massive, directed flow of water doing the physical work of separation and cleaning.

To sluice is to wash something with a strong, heavy rush of water, sweeping it clean — or, when water is the subject, to flow rapidly and powerfully in a rushing stream.

If you remember just one image: a dock worker after a long day's fishing, picking up a bucket of seawater and hurling it across a blood-and-scale-covered deck — that is sluicing.
13852: Slumber means sleep — but not just any sleep. It refers to sleep that feels peaceful, gentle, and undisturbed. Think of the quiet stillness of a child tucked in at night, or the soft rest of an afternoon nap in a hammock. That calm, tranquil quality is what gives slumber its special character.

"Sleep" is the plain, everyday word we all use. "Slumber," on the other hand, carries a softer, more poetic, almost dreamy quality. It doesn't just describe the act of sleeping — it paints a picture of stillness, comfort, and peace.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "She went to sleep." — Plain, neutral, everyday.
  • "She fell into a deep slumber." — Evokes a rich image of calm, peacefulness, and gentle rest.

Both describe the same thing, but "slumber" creates a far warmer and more vivid impression. This is why you'll find it more often in literature, poetry, fairy tales, and formal writing than in casual everyday conversation. Nobody texts their friend, "I'm heading to slumber now." But a fairy tale will absolutely say, "The princess fell into an enchanted slumber."

"Slumber" is most naturally associated with light, gentle sleep — the kind where you're resting quietly and peacefully. However, it's also very commonly used to describe deep or prolonged sleep. Phrases like "deep slumber" and "long slumber" are perfectly natural. In these cases, the word is simply emphasizing how undisturbed or complete the sleep is, not how light it is. So don't think of it as only light sleep — the emphasis is always on the peacefulness, not the depth.

Beyond literal sleep, "slumber" can be used figuratively to describe a state of inactivity, dormancy, or unawareness — when something has gone quiet, still, and stopped being active. For example:

  • "The volcano had been in slumber for centuries." — It was dormant, not erupting.
  • "The small town fell into an economic slumber." — It became inactive and stagnant.
  • "The movement finally awoke from its long slumber." — It had been inactive for a long time and was now becoming active again.

In these cases, the word borrows the idea of sleep to describe something that has temporarily stopped buzzing with life or energy. This metaphorical use is very common and important to know.

These are the natural combinations you'll encounter with "slumber":

  • Fall into a slumber — to gradually drift off to sleep.
  • Deep slumber — very heavy, sound sleep.
  • Peaceful slumber — calm, undisturbed sleep.
  • Sweet slumber — pleasant, comfortable sleep; often used affectionately.
  • Long slumber — an extended period of sleep, or metaphorically, a long period of inactivity.
  • Rouse from slumber — to wake someone up from sleep.
  • Disturb someone's slumber — to interrupt someone's sleep.

When used in the plural form, "slumbers" typically refers to a period or episode of sleep, often in a tender or poetic way. You might read "Sweet slumbers, little one" as a loving way to wish someone goodnight — it simply means peaceful sleep, expressed softly.

You'll also encounter the compound noun "slumber party," which refers to a sleepover — an occasion, usually for children or teenagers, where friends gather at someone's house and spend the night together. Despite having the word "slumber" in it, these events are famously the opposite of quiet! The name comes from the idea of sleeping over as a group.
The Overall Feel of the Word

"Slumber" is a word with a soft, warm, almost magical glow to it. It makes sleep sound like something beautiful and serene, not just a biological necessity. It belongs naturally in fairy tales, lullabies, and poetry. Whenever you read it, it signals not merely unconsciousness, but a kind of deep, undisturbed, and peaceful rest — the kind that feels safe and gentle.

In short: slumber = peaceful sleep, with a poetic quality that plain "sleep" simply doesn't carry.
13853:
To slumber means to sleep. But it is not just any kind of sleep — it is sleep that is gentle, calm, and peaceful. When someone slumbers, they are resting quietly, undisturbed, often in a soft and serene way. Think of a baby sleeping soundly in a crib, or a person drifting off peacefully on a quiet afternoon. That is slumbering.

So while "sleep" is the plain, everyday word, "slumber" carries a feeling of stillness and tranquility along with it. The act feels soft, almost dreamlike.

Both words describe the same basic act, but they feel very different in tone.

"Sleep" is neutral and factual. You use it in everyday conversation without much feeling attached to it. "I slept for eight hours." Simple, direct.

"Slumber," on the other hand, is warmer and more poetic. It paints a picture. It suggests not just that someone is asleep, but that the sleep is comfortable, undisturbed, and quiet. You would not say "I slumbered for eight hours" in a casual chat — it would sound unusual. Instead, you find "slumber" in literature, poetry, fairy tales, and writing where the writer wants to create a mood of peacefulness or beauty.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "The child slept in the room."
  • "The child slumbered in the room."

The second one feels softer, almost like you are tiptoeing around so as not to wake her.

This is where the word becomes particularly interesting and rich.

"Slumber" is also used to describe anything that is inactive, quiet, or dormant — even things that cannot literally sleep. In this figurative sense, it means to exist in a state of stillness, inactivity, or unawareness, like something that is "asleep" but not physically so.

Here are the kinds of situations where this applies:

A place can slumber. A small town that is very quiet, with little activity or movement, can be said to slumber. "The village slumbered in the summer heat." This means the town was still, quiet, and almost lifeless — like a sleeping person.

A volcano can slumber. A volcano that has not erupted for a long time is said to be slumbering. It is not dead, but it is inactive and quiet — for now. "The volcano has slumbered for three hundred years."

A problem or conflict can slumber. If a conflict or issue exists but nobody is dealing with it, and it is lying quietly under the surface, it can be said to slumber. "The old rivalry slumbered for decades before it erupted again." This means it was dormant — not gone, just not active.

A person can slumber in a figurative sense. If someone is unaware of what is happening around them, or is going through life without paying attention to important things, they can be described as slumbering. "While the danger grew, the people slumbered." Here, "slumbered" means they were oblivious, unaware — metaphorically "asleep."

One important thing to understand about this word is the mood it creates. When a writer chooses "slumber" instead of "sleep," it is usually intentional. The word has a hushed, quiet quality to it — almost like a whisper. It creates a sense of calm, peace, and sometimes even mystery.

This is why you see it so often in fairy tales. "Sleeping Beauty slumbered under the spell" sounds far more enchanting than "Sleeping Beauty slept under the spell." The word itself feels like a lullaby.

It can also carry a sense of vulnerability — someone who is slumbering is completely unguarded, at rest, unaware of the world. This is why the figurative use (a people slumbering while danger approaches) works so powerfully: it carries the weight of that same defencelessness.

As a verb, it follows normal patterns and is easy to use in any tense.

  • Present: "She slumbers." / "They slumber."
  • Past: "He slumbered through the storm."
  • Progressive (ongoing action): "The old city is slumbering under the snow."
  • Perfect: "The threat has slumbered long enough."

It can be used with adverbs to add texture: "slumbered peacefully," "slumbered fitfully" (which would actually be somewhat unusual and ironic, given the word's gentle nature), or "slumbered quietly."
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

To slumber is to sleep — but specifically in a gentle, peaceful, undisturbed way. Beyond its literal meaning, it is used figuratively to describe anything — a place, a force, a conflict, a person's awareness — that is inactive, dormant, or quietly at rest. It is a word of mood and atmosphere, chosen when a writer wants to create a feeling of stillness, beauty, or quiet. It lives most naturally in literature, poetry, and descriptive writing rather than everyday casual speech.

If you remember one thing: wherever there is quietness, peacefulness, and a kind of beautiful stillness — whether in a sleeping person or a sleeping world — that is where "slumber" belongs.
13854:
A slump is a significant, noticeable fall or drop — in performance, numbers, energy, or activity — that lasts for a period of time. It is not a tiny dip. It is not a single bad moment. It is a stretch of doing badly or a sharp decline that you can clearly see and feel.

Think of it this way: imagine a graph that was going well or staying stable, and then it suddenly drops down and stays low for a while. That low period — that fall and the time spent in it — is the slump.

1. A period of poor performance

This is the most personal use of the word. When a person, a team, or a business is going through a run of bad results — performing well below their usual standard — that is a slump.

  • A basketball player who normally scores 25 points a game suddenly can't seem to score for three weeks. He is in a slump.
  • A writer who used to produce great work every week suddenly struggles to write anything decent for two months. She is in a creative slump.
  • A sales team that used to close 50 deals a month is now closing 15. The team is in a slump.

The word is especially common in sports, where players and teams can go through frustrating stretches of underperformance.

2. A sharp drop in numbers or values

Here, "slump" refers to a steep, significant fall in something measurable — prices, sales, demand, profits, or economic activity.

  • There was a slump in house prices after the financial crisis.
  • The company reported a slump in sales during the winter months.
  • Consumer demand fell sharply — a slump that worried investors.

In this sense, it's not just that things went down slightly. A slump implies the drop was notable and serious.

3. An economic downturn

On a larger scale, "slump" is used to describe a period when an entire economy is performing badly — with slow growth, falling output, high unemployment, and low consumer spending.

  • The country entered an economic slump after the crash.
  • The Great Depression is sometimes called the Great Slump.

This is similar to a recession but is a more general, informal term. It captures the idea of the whole economy feeling heavy and sluggish.
The Key Feeling of the Word

What makes "slump" special is the combination of three qualities:

  1. Suddenness or sharpness — things didn't fade slowly; they dropped noticeably.
  2. Duration — it's not one bad day. It's a bad period — days, weeks, months.
  3. Expectation of recovery — a slump implies something was better before, and could be better again. It feels temporary, even if painful.

This is why "slump" has a particular emotional weight. It describes the frustrating, heavy experience of things going wrong for a sustained stretch of time, when you know they were once better.

PhraseMeaning

"In a slump" — Currently going through a bad period.
"The whole team has been in a slump this month."

"Hit a slump" — To enter a slump; the moment things start going badly.
"He hit a slump after his injury."

"Fall into a slump" — Similar to "hit a slump," but suggests a gradual descent.
"After losing her job, she fell into a slump."

"Come out of a slump" / "snap out of a slump" — To start recovering and performing well again.
"The striker finally came out of his slump and scored twice."

"A slump in [something]" — A drop in a specific thing.
"There's been a slump in tourism this year."

Slump vs. Dip:
A dip is small and brief. A slump is serious and sustained. If sales fall 2% for a week, that's a dip. If they fall 30% for three months, that's a slump.

Slump vs. Crash:
A crash is violent, sudden, and often catastrophic — think of a stock market crash. A slump is also a fall, but it's more prolonged and carries the sense of things being dragged down and stuck low, rather than hitting a wall instantly.

Slump vs. Decline:
A decline is often gradual and steady — a slow downward slope over a long time. A slump is sharper and more dramatic. Companies in long-term decline are fading; a company in a slump has dropped hard and fast.

Slump vs. Rut:
A rut means being stuck doing the same thing repeatedly, trapped in routine. A slump is about performing badly or things going poorly. You can be in a rut while still succeeding — you just feel stuck. A slump always involves clearly worse results.

A slump (noun) is:

  • A significant drop in performance, numbers, or economic activity.
  • That lasts for a period of time — not just a single bad moment.
  • It implies things were better before and could hopefully be better again.
  • It can apply to a person (sports, work, creativity), a business (sales, profits), or an entire economy.

The single clearest sentence to remember it: A slump is what happens when something that was going well falls hard and stays low for a while.
13855:
To slump means to fall, sink, or drop in a heavy, limp, and lifeless way — as if all strength or support has suddenly been drained away. The key image behind this word is something giving way under its own weight, without control or energy. Think of a puppet whose strings have been cut. That heavy, drooping collapse? That is what "slump" feels like.

It has two main areas of meaning — one physical (what bodies do) and one figurative (what numbers, performance, or conditions do) — but the same core feeling runs through both: a sudden, significant sinking downward, with a sense of defeat or failure in the air.
Meaning 1 — Physical: When a Body Falls or Sinks Heavily

When a person (or their body part) slumps, they fall or sink into a drooping, slouched, heavy position — usually because they are exhausted, deeply sad, relieved, unconscious, injured, or completely defeated.

Examples:

  • She slumped into the sofa after the long shift and didn't move for an hour. (She sank into it with all her weight, with no energy left.)
  • He slumped against the wall and slid to the floor. (His body gave way; he couldn't hold himself up.)
  • When she heard the bad news, her shoulders slumped. (Her shoulders dropped forward and downward — a physical signal of sadness or defeat.)
  • The drunk man slumped over the table. (He fell forward heavily, lifelessly.)
  • The soldier was found slumped in the corner, unconscious. (His body had collapsed without control.)

What makes slump special here: It is not just falling. It is a heavy, limp, ungraceful fall — the kind that happens when a person stops fighting gravity. It carries a feeling of loss of control, loss of energy, or defeat. A person who slumps is not standing tall. Their body is giving up.

Notice that you can slump your whole body, or just a part of your body:

  • Shoulders slumped → sadness or defeat.
  • Head slumped forward → sleep or unconsciousness.
  • Body slumped → exhaustion, injury, or grief.
Meaning 2 — Figurative: When Numbers, Performance, or Conditions Fall Sharply

This is the other major use of "slump." Here, it means to fall or decline suddenly, significantly, and noticeably — often in a way that is worrying or disappointing. This is very common in business, economics, and sports.

Examples:

  • Sales slumped by 40% after the scandal. (They fell sharply and suddenly.)
  • The stock market slumped overnight. (Prices dropped heavily.)
  • Her confidence slumped after the failed presentation. (It dropped significantly; she felt deflated.)
  • Profits slumped to their lowest point in a decade. (They fell to a very low level.)
  • Attendance at the games has slumped this season. (Numbers have fallen noticeably.)

What makes slump special here: Other words like "fall" or "drop" are neutral — they just describe movement downward. But slump carries weight and drama. When something slumps, it doesn't just go down a little — it goes down in a way that feels significant, heavy, and often alarming. It suggests the decline was notable enough to be a problem.
A Special Use: "Going Through a Slump"

In everyday life, especially in sports, you will often hear people say someone is slumping or going through a slump. Here, it means they are performing poorly over a stretch of time — not just one bad day, but a sustained period of difficulty.

Examples:

  • The basketball player has been slumping all month — he can't seem to score. (He's in a bad run of form.)
  • I've been slumping at work lately; nothing seems to go right. (He's performing below his usual level.)
  • Even the best athletes slump from time to time. (They go through periods of poor performance.)

This use blends both meanings: just like a body that slumps loses its strength and posture, a person or team that is slumping has lost their usual energy, form, or output.

This is important: slump is never a proud or neutral word. It almost always carries a feeling of:

  • Defeat — like losing a battle.
  • Exhaustion — like running out of fuel.
  • Disappointment — something fell short of what it should be.
  • Helplessness — the falling happened without the person being able to stop it.

When a writer chooses "slump" instead of a simpler word like "fall" or "drop," they are deliberately painting a picture of something going down in a heavy, sad, or alarming way. It adds emotional weight.

These distinctions will sharpen your understanding significantly.

Slump vs. Drop:
"Drop" is clean and neutral. Prices dropped. Slump is heavier and more dramatic. Prices slumped suggests a more worrying, significant fall — and feels more vivid.

Slump vs. Collapse:
"Collapse" is sudden and total — like a building falling down all at once. "Slump" is heavy and significant, but not necessarily total. A slumped body still has some shape; a collapsed building is completely undone. Also, collapse feels more catastrophic than slump.

Slump vs. Slouch:
"Slouch" is about habitual, lazy bad posture — someone who always sits or walks with their shoulders rounded forward. "Slump" is more dramatic — it is the act of suddenly sinking heavily, often due to an emotion or loss of consciousness. You slouch every day; you slump in a specific, charged moment.

Slump vs. Sink:
"Sink" is gentler and slower — she sank into the chair with a sigh. "Slump" is heavier and more abrupt — she slumped into the chair, exhausted. Slump has more weight and drama to it.

• Slump into something: She slumped into the couch.
  • Slump against something: He slumped against the door.
  • Slump over something: She slumped over her desk.
  • Slump down: He slumped down in his chair.
  • Slumped shoulders / a slumped figure: Visual descriptions of a person whose posture shows defeat or sadness.
  • Slump by X%: Profits slumped by 20%.
  • Slump to a low / to the lowest / to a record low: Sales slumped to their lowest in five years.

Slump (verb) = to fall, sink, or decline in a heavy, limp, or significant way — whether it is a body giving way to exhaustion or defeat, or a number/performance falling sharply. Whenever you see or use this word, the feeling behind it is always the same: something that had strength, height, or energy has lost it — and dropped.
13856: Before jumping into the different meanings, here's the thread that connects all of them: a slur always involves something being blurred, smeared, or dragged in a way that causes damage or loss of clarity — whether it's someone's reputation, a group's dignity, or the clarity of sounds in speech or music. Keep that idea in mind as you read through the meanings below.
Meaning 1: An Offensive Word or Statement (the most common meaning)

This is the meaning most people encounter most often. A slur is a word, phrase, or remark that attacks or degrades a person or a group of people — usually based on something about their identity, such as their race, religion, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, or disability.

A slur doesn't just criticize someone. It dehumanizes them. It reduces an entire group of people to a stereotype, treating their identity as something shameful or inferior. This is what makes slurs different from ordinary insults. A regular insult attacks what someone did. A slur attacks what someone is.

For example: A racial slur is a word used to demean someone because of their race. Such words carry a long history of hatred and discrimination, which is a big part of why they cause such deep harm.

You'll often hear the phrase "hurling a slur" or "using a slur", which captures how these words are thrown at people like weapons.

A few important points to understand the full picture:

  • Context matters enormously. Some communities have reclaimed slurs that were once used against them, using the words among themselves in a way that strips the hatred out of them. However, the same word used by an outsider, or used with hostile intent, remains a slur in the harmful sense.
  • A slur doesn't have to be a single word. It can be a phrase or remark that implies inferiority or contempt toward a group.
  • Slurs cause real harm. Research consistently shows that being targeted by slurs causes psychological distress, feelings of exclusion, and lasting emotional damage. This is why they are treated as a serious matter in law, workplace policy, and social life.
Meaning 2: A Stain on Someone's Reputation

In a more formal or old-fashioned sense, a slur is a damaging claim or suggestion made against a person's character or reputation, often one that is unfair or unproven.

For example: "The accusation was a slur on his reputation that he never fully recovered from."

Think of it like a muddy smear on a clean surface. Even after you wipe it away, a trace often remains. That's what a reputational slur does — it leaves a mark of suspicion or shame on how others perceive a person. This meaning overlaps closely with Meaning 1, but it is broader because it doesn't have to involve identity-based hatred. It can simply be a false or malicious claim that damages how someone is seen publicly.
Meaning 3: A Curved Mark in Written Music

This meaning is completely unrelated to insults. In the world of music, a slur is a curved line drawn above or below a group of notes in written music (sheet music). It tells the performer to play or sing those notes smoothly and connected, flowing from one note to the next without any gap or break between them. This style of playing is called legato (a term from Italian meaning "tied together").

For example: A singer seeing a slur over five notes knows to sing those five notes in one smooth, unbroken breath, almost melting one into the next.

A slur is different from a tie, which is a similar-looking curved line but only connects two notes of the same pitch, simply extending the duration of that one note. A slur, by contrast, connects notes of different pitches and is purely an instruction about smoothness and connection.
Meaning 4: A Blurring of Sounds in Speech

A slur can also refer to the act or result of running speech sounds together in a way that makes words unclear or hard to understand. When someone speaks very quickly, is extremely tired, or is under the influence of alcohol or certain medications, their words may lose their sharp edges and blur into each other. The resulting unclear, mushy speech can itself be called a slur — or the unclear sounds are said to be "slurred."

For example: "His speech came out as a slur — nobody could make out what he was saying."
How All the Meanings Fit Together

Now you can see why that one core idea — smearing, blurring, dragging — holds all these meanings together.

  • An offensive slur smears a person's dignity or identity.
  • A reputational slur smears a person's good name.
  • A musical slur drags notes together in a smooth, connected flow.
  • A speech slur drags sounds together until they lose their clarity.

The word wears different clothes in different contexts, but the same underlying sense runs through all of them.

ContextWhat "slur" means
Everyday languageAn offensive, dehumanizing word targeting someone's identity
Formal/legal languageA damaging, unfair claim against someone's reputation
MusicA curved line instructing smooth, connected performance of notes
SpeechA blurring of sounds that makes words unclear
13857: "Slur" as a verb has a small family of related meanings. Think of them as branches of the same tree — they all share a common idea of blending, blurring, or dragging something carelessly or smoothly.
Meaning 1: To speak unclearly by blending words together

This is the most common meaning you'll encounter in daily life.

When someone slurs their words, they don't pronounce them clearly and crisply. Instead, the words melt into each other in a sloppy, blurred way, making them hard to understand. The sounds are not sharp or well-separated — they slide together.

This typically happens when someone is:

  • Drunk (the most classic case — alcohol weakens muscle control, including the tongue and lips)
  • Extremely tired or drowsy
  • Having a medical emergency, like a stroke (sudden slurring of speech is actually a warning sign doctors take seriously)
  • Heavily medicated or under the influence of certain drugs

Examples:

  • "He had too much to drink, and by midnight he was slurring so badly we could barely understand him."
  • "The patient's speech began to slur, so they rushed her to the hospital."
  • "She was so exhausted after the 36-hour shift that she was slurring through her sentences."

Notice that the target of this verb is almost always words or speech. You slur your words, or your speech slurs.
Meaning 2: To pass over something hastily and carelessly (often "slur over")

This meaning is slightly less common but very useful to know.

When you slur over something, you treat it in a rushed, careless, superficial way. You skim past it without giving it the proper time, attention, or detail it deserves — almost as if you're hoping no one notices you're being lazy or evasive about it.

Examples:

  • "The politician slurred over the most controversial part of his proposal, giving it just one vague sentence."
  • "The teacher slurred over the difficult chapter because the exam was the next day and there was no time."
  • "She noticed that the report slurred over the financial losses, burying them in confusing language."

Think of it like a paintbrush dragging quickly across a surface — you've covered it, but not properly. There's no depth, no care.
Meaning 3: To damage or attack someone's reputation

When you slur a person, you say things that are harmful, insulting, or damaging to how others see them. You smear their character or reputation — often unfairly or falsely.

This sense of the verb is closely related to the noun slur (an offensive remark or accusation), and the two feed into each other.

Examples:

  • "The rival campaign tried to slur the candidate by spreading false stories about his past."
  • "She felt the article was deliberately designed to slur her character."
  • "He had spent years building a good name, and a single rumour was enough to slur it."

The key idea here is deliberate harm to reputation — someone is using words as weapons to make others think badly of a person.
Meaning 4: In music — to play or sing notes in a smooth, connected flow

This is a technical musical meaning, but it's worth knowing.

When a musician slurs a group of notes, they perform them in one smooth, unbroken, flowing phrase — without any gap, pause, or hard separation between the notes. Each note connects seamlessly into the next, like one continuous, liquid movement.

This is the opposite of playing notes in a clipped, detached, or separate style (called staccato). Slurred notes are joined; staccato notes are separated.

In written music, a curved line called a slur mark is drawn over or under a group of notes to tell the performer: "Connect these smoothly."

Examples:

  • "The cellist slurred the passage beautifully, giving it a warm, singing quality."
  • "The phrase should be slurred, not played note by note — make it sound like one breath."

Here, interestingly, "slurring" is not a bad thing at all — it's a deliberate, skilled technique.

It helps to see the thread running through all four meanings:

MeaningThe core idea
Slurring speechSounds blur and blend together carelessly
Slurring over somethingAttention slides past without stopping properly
Slurring a personSharp, clear reputation becomes smeared and muddy
Slurring notes (music)Notes blend into one smooth, connected line

In every case, something that could be crisp, clear, or precise is instead blended, smeared, or rushed — whether for bad reasons (drunken speech, laziness, malice) or for a deliberate artistic reason (music).

Think of the word smear as your closest friend to "slur." Whether it's sounds, attention, reputation, or musical notes — to slur something is to smear it: to make its edges unclear, to drag it messily, or to blur the distinctions that would otherwise be crisp.
13858:
If someone is sly, they are clever in a hidden, secretive way — they get what they want through quiet tricks, secret plans, or subtle deception, without others noticing what they are really doing.

Think of it this way: a smart person solves a problem openly. A sly person solves it in the shadows.

To truly understand "sly," you need to see the three ideas that live inside it at the same time:

1. Cleverness — A sly person is not stupid. They are sharp. They think ahead and plan carefully.

2. Secrecy — Their cleverness is hidden. They don't show their true intentions. They let others believe one thing while they are quietly doing another.

3. A slightly tricky or mischievous quality — There is always a sense that a sly person is operating just outside the rules, or bending them, even if they don't break them completely.

All three must be present. A person who is only secretive is just shy or private. A person who is only clever is just intelligent. When you combine hidden cleverness with a tricky motive — that is "sly."

In stories and culture across the world, the fox is the universal symbol of slyness. Why? Because a fox doesn't attack a chicken coop with brute force. It quietly observes, finds the weak spot, sneaks in without making a sound, takes what it wants, and disappears — and you only discover it happened after the fact. That quiet, clever, under-the-radar way of operating — that is slyness in its purest form.

Not always — and this is important to understand.

"Sly" sits on a spectrum:

  • On the negative end, a sly person is manipulative, deceptive, and untrustworthy. They use their hidden cleverness to cheat, mislead, or take advantage of people. This is the most common use.
  • In the middle, "sly" can describe someone who is quietly cunning in a way that's impressive rather than morally wrong — like a negotiator who keeps their cards close to their chest and wins a deal without revealing their strategy.
  • On the lighter end, "sly" is used with a kind of admiration or playful affection. If someone finds a clever loophole that makes everyone laugh, you might say, "You sly thing!" — almost as a compliment. This usage is less common but real.

So the word carries a negative flavour by default, but context can soften it all the way to a friendly tease.
The "Sly" Look — A Very Common Usage

One of the most frequent ways "sly" is used is to describe a facial expression or a glance:

  • a sly smile
  • a sly grin
  • a sly look
  • a sly wink

These expressions all describe the same thing: a subtle, knowing expression that says "I know something you don't" or "I'm up to something, and I won't tell you what." It's not a big, open laugh. It's quiet. Controlled. Hidden at the corners. That restraint — the fact that it doesn't give everything away — is exactly what makes it sly.

• A coworker who quietly takes credit for your idea in a meeting, without anyone realizing what they did — that person is sly.
  • A child who knows their parent is in the next room, waits for the perfect silent moment, sneaks a biscuit from the jar, and walks back to their seat looking completely innocent — that is a sly move.
  • A poker player who lets others think they have a weak hand, while quietly setting up a trap to win everything — sly.
  • A friend who arranges a surprise party for you, asks you a hundred innocent-sounding questions to figure out your plans, and never once gives anything away — you might call them sly afterward, probably while laughing.

These words are related, but each has its own flavour:

Cunning — Very close to sly, but "cunning" leans more strongly negative and implies a sharper, more calculated type of manipulation. All cunning people are sly, but a sly person isn't always cunning — they might just be quietly mischievous.

Sneaky — Focuses on the action of doing things in secret. A sneaky person hides what they are doing. A sly person hides what they are thinking and planning. Sly is deeper — it's about the mind behind the behavior.

Crafty — Emphasizes skill and ingenuity, like a craftsman. A crafty person finds clever solutions. It's similar to sly but slightly more neutral — "crafty" doesn't carry as much of the deceptive edge.

Devious — More seriously negative than sly. A devious person has genuinely bad intentions and goes through twisted, roundabout means to achieve them. "Sly" is lighter; "devious" is darker.

This is a very common phrase you will encounter. "On the sly" means doing something in secret, usually something you don't want others to know about.

  • She was texting him on the sly.
  • He was eating sweets on the sly even though the doctor told him to stop.

The phrase captures the same essence: something hidden, something slightly sneaky, happening underneath the surface.

Sly means clever in a quiet, secretive, and slightly tricky way — a sly person always seems to know more than they let on, and they use that hidden knowledge to their own advantage, often without others ever realising what just happened.
13859:
Small talk is light, casual conversation about unimportant topics that people have with each other — especially with people they don't know well, or in social situations where a deeper conversation would feel awkward or out of place.

The word "small" here means not serious or not significant — not physically small. And "talk" simply means conversation. So small talk = a small, light conversation.
What Small Talk Actually Looks and Feels Like

Small talk is the kind of conversation where nobody is really exchanging important information. Instead, it's more about being friendly, filling a silence, or simply acknowledging another person warmly. It stays on the surface. It doesn't go deep.

Here are some real-life examples of small talk:

  • "Nice weather today, isn't it?"
  • "How was your weekend?"
  • "Did you catch the game last night?"
  • "This coffee is really good!"
  • "Are you from around here?"

Notice how none of these questions are trying to solve a problem, learn something critical, or discuss anything serious. They are simply friendly, easy exchanges.

Even though small talk seems pointless at first glance, it actually serves very important social functions:

1. It breaks the ice.
When two people don't know each other well — like strangers in an elevator, or new colleagues at a workplace — silence can feel uncomfortable. Small talk dissolves that awkwardness and makes both people feel at ease.

2. It builds connection.
Small talk is the first step toward a relationship. You don't start a friendship by immediately discussing your deepest fears. You start with small talk, and over time, as trust grows, conversations naturally become deeper.

3. It shows friendliness and respect.
Making small talk with someone signals: "I see you. I acknowledge you. I'm approachable." Refusing to make small talk can sometimes come across as cold or rude, even if that's not the intention.

4. It maintains social bonds.
Even between people who know each other, small talk helps maintain the relationship during moments when there's nothing major to discuss — like bumping into a neighbor on the street.

Small talk is extremely common in everyday life. You'll find it in situations like:

  • Waiting in a queue or an elevator
  • The beginning of a work meeting (before it officially starts)
  • At a party, especially with people you've just met
  • At a hair salon, barbershop, or during a taxi ride
  • When meeting a friend-of-a-friend for the first time
  • At family gatherings, between relatives who aren't very close

These are all situations where a deep, serious conversation would feel strange or forced, but saying nothing would feel cold. Small talk fills that gap perfectly.

Certain topics are considered universally "safe" and popular for small talk because they are unlikely to offend anyone or lead to disagreement. These include:

  • The weather — the most classic small talk topic in the world
  • Weekend plans or recent activities — "Any fun plans this weekend?"
  • Sports — especially local teams or recent big events
  • Food — "Have you tried that new restaurant on 5th Street?"
  • Light current events — things that are not controversial
  • Compliments — "I love your bag!" or "That's a great idea!"
  • Work or school — very general questions like "How's work been lately?"

Topics that are avoided in small talk include religion, politics, money, personal relationships, health problems, and anything deeply personal — these topics can easily create tension or discomfort, which is the opposite of what small talk is meant to do.

Small talk has a specific tone: it is warm, light, positive, and non-committal. People usually don't give deeply honest or detailed answers during small talk, and that's perfectly normal and accepted.

For example, if someone asks "How are you?" as small talk, they don't necessarily want a full, detailed answer about your life. The socially expected answer is something simple and positive like "I'm good, thanks! How about you?" — even if you're having a hard day. This isn't considered dishonest; it's simply the understood social contract of small talk.

It helps to understand small talk by comparing it to its opposite:

Small TalkDeep/Meaningful Conversation
TopicsLight, safe, generalPersonal, serious, significant
PurposeSocial comfort, connectionSharing, problem-solving, bonding
DepthSurface levelGoes beneath the surface
Example"Nice weather!""I've been feeling really lost in my career lately."

Small talk is not inferior to deep conversation — it simply serves a different and equally important role in human social life.
"Make Small Talk" — The Most Common Phrase

In everyday English, the most natural and common way to use this noun is in the phrase "make small talk."

  • "We made small talk while waiting for the bus."
  • "I'm not very good at making small talk at parties."
  • "They made small talk for a few minutes before getting to the point."

You will hear and read this phrase constantly in English. The verb "make" is almost always the verb that pairs with "small talk."

Small talk is casual, friendly conversation about light and unimportant topics. It happens between strangers, acquaintances, or even friends in social situations where serious conversation isn't expected. Its purpose is not to exchange meaningful information, but to create comfort, signal friendliness, and gently build human connection. It is a fundamental and universal part of social life.
